composer.name: François Couperin
composer.epithet: A Parisian organist whose harpsichord pieces turn ornament, delayed resolution and the timing of a released key into structural events.
facts: Nephew of Louis Couperin; succeeded his father Charles at Saint-Gervais
Organist of Saint-Gervais from 1685; royal chapel organist from 1693; royal chamber harpsichordist from 1717
Four books of harpsichord pieces, 27 ordres; organ masses, chamber music, motets and Leçons de Ténèbres
composer.background:
François Couperin belonged to a family whose connection with the organ of Saint-Gervais in Paris lasted for generations. His father Charles died in 1679, when François was ten; Michel-Richard de Lalande temporarily held the post intended for the boy. Couperin took it up in 1685. His uncle Louis, who had died before François was born, had already established a distinctive harpsichord language of broken chords, dance rhythms and unmeasured preludes. The younger Couperin inherited a profession and a repertory. His own published harpsichord music would increasingly substitute named character pieces for a predictable succession of dances.

In 1693 he won one of the four organist positions at Louis XIV’s royal chapel. Serving by quarter, he combined court employment with his Parisian responsibilities. He taught members of the royal family and took part in chamber performances; in 1717 he became a royal chamber harpsichordist. These overlapping appointments help explain his range: a musician who supplied an organ verset for a service might also teach the fingering of an ornament or play a concert with violin and viol.

composer.name: Antonio Vivaldi
composer.epithet: A violinist and theatre composer who made the returning orchestral refrain organise a soloist’s changing keys, textures and physical risks.
facts: Violin with his father Giovanni Battista, a violinist at St Mark’s, Venice
Violin teacher at the Ospedale della Pietà from 1703; maestro de’ concerti from 1716; theatre work in Venice and other cities
More than 500 concertos; operas, sacred vocal music, sonatas and chamber cantatas
composer.background:
Vivaldi was born in Venice, the son of a barber who became a professional violinist at St Mark’s. Giovanni Battista Vivaldi taught his son the violin and remained involved in his musical work. Antonio trained for the priesthood and was ordained in 1703, acquiring the nickname il prete rosso, the red priest, from his hair. He soon ceased regularly celebrating Mass, later explaining that a condition of tightness in the chest prevented him. He travelled extensively, taught and managed operatic productions.

In 1703 the Ospedale della Pietà appointed him violin teacher. The Pietà was a charitable institution that cared for abandoned children; its celebrated performing body consisted of girls and women whose training could continue into adult professional responsibility within the institution. Concerts and services attracted Venetian patrons and foreign visitors. Vivaldi’s employment was periodically renewed and sometimes interrupted, but the connection endured for decades. The players supplied a practical laboratory: a concerto could be written for a particular instrumental skill, tried in performance, and followed by another that changed the problem.

composer.name: Jean-Philippe Rameau
composer.epithet: A theorist of chord roots who began his operatic career at fifty and made harmonic surprise part of French theatrical action.
facts: Organist in French provincial cities, including Clermont-Ferrand; first harpsichord book published in 1706
Traité de l’harmonie, 1722; Nouveau système de musique théorique, 1726
First opera, Hippolyte et Aricie, 1733; tragédies en musique, opéras-ballets and court entertainments
composer.background:
Rameau was born in Dijon, where his father worked as an organist. The documentation of his first four decades is much thinner than that of his Parisian operatic career. He held church appointments in several French cities, published a first book of harpsichord pieces in Paris in 1706, and worked again at Clermont-Ferrand before settling permanently in the capital in the early 1720s. Keyboards, church duties and the analysis of musical practice formed his training. By the time he wrote his first surviving opera he had already published the theoretical book for which his name was known.

The Traité de l’harmonie réduite à ses principes naturels appeared in 1722. Rameau proposed that chords and their connections could be understood through a fundamental bass. Inversion became central: a chord could retain its identity while one of its upper notes moved into the bass. His explanations developed across later books, and his claims to a foundation in nature changed as he engaged with acoustics. The theory attempts to explain why harmonic progressions cohere.

composer.name: Johann Sebastian Bach
composer.epithet: An organist, teacher and church musician who made a bass line, a dance rhythm and a fugue subject carry the same argument.
facts: Family musicians in Eisenach and Ohrdruf; school at Lüneburg; study of German, French and Italian scores
Arnstadt · Mühlhausen · Weimar · Köthen · Thomaskantor in Leipzig, 1723–50
Organ, harpsichord, clavichord and violin; an examiner of organs and a teacher of keyboard players
Cantatas, Passions, the B minor Mass, organ and keyboard cycles, concertos, unaccompanied string music
composer.background:
Bach was born into a family of professional musicians in Eisenach, where his father Johann Ambrosius served as a town musician. The surname already meant a trade: relatives supplied organists, cantors and instrumentalists across Thuringia. His mother died in 1694 and his father in 1695; at ten he went to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist in Ohrdruf who had studied with Pachelbel. Keyboard instruction belonged to that household, alongside school and choir. In 1700 Bach travelled to Lüneburg, where a place in the choir of St Michael’s school gave a boy without substantial means access to an education and a musical library.

The early career was practical and local. After a brief appointment at Weimar, he became organist of the New Church in Arnstadt in 1703, with a recently built instrument to test and play. His duties included working with students, and the town’s records preserve disputes over both his behaviour and his music. In 1705 he obtained leave to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck and stayed away much longer than authorised. Buxtehude’s organ works offered a model in which free passagework, recurring basses and strict counterpoint could occupy the same piece. Bach’s own organ preludes would retain that alternation between improvisatory display and composed argument.

composer.name: George Frideric Handel
composer.epithet: A German-trained composer of Italian opera who made the English chorus an actor in public musical drama.
facts: With Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow in Halle; theatre work in Hamburg; study and commissions in Italy, 1706–10
Hanover briefly; settled in London in 1712; became a British subject in 1727
Italian operas, English oratorios, anthems, concertos, chamber cantatas and ceremonial orchestral music
composer.background:
Handel grew up in Halle, the son of a barber-surgeon, and studied with Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow, organist of the town’s principal church. Zachow’s teaching included counterpoint, keyboard playing and the copying of other composers’ music. Handel briefly enrolled at the university and held an organist’s post before moving to Hamburg in 1703. Its public opera house offered a different education: he played in the orchestra and encountered the practical demands of singers, stage machinery and mixed theatrical repertory. His first opera, Almira, was performed there in 1705, with a German text incorporating Italian arias.

From 1706 to 1710 Handel worked in Italy, writing cantatas, sacred music and opera for patrons in Florence, Rome, Naples and Venice. Rome gave him access to virtuoso singers and to instrumentalists associated with Corelli. The Latin Dixit Dominus of 1707 demands rapid, independent choral lines and sustained control of dissonance; the chamber cantatas make emotional turns within much smaller forces. Agrippina, performed in Venice at the end of 1709, assembles much previously written material into a calculated theatrical comedy. Reuse was already part of his method: a successful musical gesture could acquire a different function when assigned to a new character and situation.

composer.name: Domenico Scarlatti
composer.epithet: An Italian court musician in Lisbon and Madrid who made keyboard sonatas out of hand crossings, repeated notes and abrupt changes of harmonic ground.
facts: Son of the opera composer Alessandro Scarlatti; born in the same year as Bach and Handel
Naples and Rome; Portuguese royal service from 1719; followed Maria Bárbara to Spain in 1729
555 keyboard sonatas in Ralph Kirkpatrick’s catalogue; earlier operas, cantatas and sacred music
composer.background:
Domenico Scarlatti was born in Naples, the sixth child of Alessandro Scarlatti, an established composer of opera and sacred music. He entered professional musical life as a teenager, working as an organist and composing for the stage. Domenico eventually concentrated on keyboard music in courts far from Naples, taking a different path from his father’s large operatic career. His first decades included church appointments, singers, theatrical commissions and the practical education of a musician expected to supply whatever his employer required.

In Rome he worked for the exiled Polish queen Maria Casimira and at St Peter’s, writing both opera and sacred music. The ten-part Stabat Mater, usually associated with these Roman years, combines four soprano lines with pairs of altos, tenors and basses. Its voices enter in changing combinations, and the density of the counterpoint can contract around a particular text.

intro: A keyboard sonata built from repeated attacks, changes of register and chords containing notes that refuse to agree. Its two repeated halves give Scarlatti room to make the same disturbances lead towards different keys.

composer.name: Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach
composer.epithet: A keyboard player who made hesitation, interruption and a change of mind into musical form.
facts: With his father, Johann Sebastian Bach; law studies at Leipzig and Frankfurt an der Oder
Keyboard player to Frederick II in Berlin and Potsdam, 1740–67 · Hamburg music director, 1768–88
Versuch über die wahre Art das Clavier zu spielen, 1753 and 1762
Wq = Alfred Wotquenne; H = E. Eugene Helm
composer.background:
Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach was the second surviving son of Johann Sebastian Bach and Maria Barbara Bach. He was born in Weimar in 1714; Georg Philipp Telemann was one of his godfathers. The family moved to Cöthen in 1717 and Leipzig in 1723, where his father became Thomaskantor. Emanuel learned the keyboard and composition at home, then studied law at Leipzig and Frankfurt an der Oder. He made music his profession: by 1738 he had entered the circle of the Prussian crown prince Frederick, who became king in 1740.

Frederick played the flute, composed and maintained an orchestra whose leading musicians included Johann Joachim Quantz and the brothers Graun. Bach’s employment was chiefly as a keyboard accompanist. In his own publications he pursued a style independent of the king’s Italianate melodic preferences. His six ‘Prussian’ keyboard sonatas of 1742 and six ‘Württemberg’ sonatas of 1744 put contrasting textures, unexpected rests and highly ornamented slow movements inside the three-movement sonata. The player had to manage changes of character as precisely as changes of fingering.

intro: A clavichord can alter a note after the finger has struck it. In this late fantasia, Bach makes an instrument quiet enough for a private room speak in interruptions, pauses and sudden changes of register.

composer.name: Joseph Haydn
composer.epithet: A court musician who taught the symphony and quartet to argue with the listener’s expectations.
facts: Choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral, Vienna; practical instruction from Nicola Porpora
Esterházy household, 1761–1809; active court duties reduced after 1790
Visits in 1791–92 and 1794–95; twelve symphonies for the English public
104 numbered symphonies · string quartets · keyboard sonatas and trios · masses · operas · oratorios
composer.background:
Haydn was born in Rohrau, near the border between Lower Austria and Hungary, in 1732. His father was a wheelwright who sang and played the harp by ear; his mother had worked as a cook. Music began at home. After early schooling in Hainburg, he became a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. The work gave him daily experience of church music and a singer’s understanding of phrases, but little systematic composition teaching. When his voice broke, he lost the position and had to earn his living outside the cathedral.

In the 1750s he taught, accompanied and played whatever engagements he could obtain. Working for the singing teacher and composer Nicola Porpora gave him practical instruction in Italian vocal style. He studied scores and keyboard music, including the sonatas of C. P. E. Bach, whose sudden contrasts offered another model besides the regular phrases of the fashionable galant style. Employment by Count Morzin in the late 1750s brought an orchestra and the first symphonies. In 1760 he married Maria Anna Keller; the marriage was unhappy and childless. His professional stability came from a different household.

intro: The loud chord is only the first interruption. Haydn takes a tune made from a few notes of C major through four variations, changing its scoring, mode and rhythmic density without losing its outline.

composer.name: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
composer.epithet: An opera composer whose instrumental music gives different voices the freedom to disagree.
facts: By his father Leopold; extensive performing tours from childhood
Salzburg · Italy · Mannheim and Paris · Vienna from 1781
Italian opera seria and opera buffa; German Singspiel with spoken dialogue
K. or KV = Ludwig von Köchel’s catalogue, first published in 1862 and repeatedly revised
composer.background:
Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, the seventh child of Leopold Mozart and Anna Maria Pertl; only he and his sister Maria Anna survived infancy. Leopold was a violinist and composer in the archbishop’s service, and in the year of Wolfgang’s birth published an influential violin treatise. He taught both children. Maria Anna, called Nannerl within the family, became an accomplished keyboard player, and the first tours presented brother and sister together. The family’s travels were an educational system as well as a business: the children encountered instruments, performers, repertories and audiences that a Salzburg childhood alone could not have supplied.

The long tour of 1763–66 took them through German courts, Paris, London and the Netherlands. In London Mozart met Johann Christian Bach, whose clear phrases and Italianate melodic style offered a model different from the contrapuntal teaching associated with Bach’s father. Illness repeatedly interrupted the itinerary. Leopold managed engagements, publicity and money while supervising composition, and the surviving correspondence documents the costs and uncertainties behind the public demonstrations. Wolfgang learned to write for named performers and immediate occasions before he had an independent adult household.

composer.name: Ludwig van Beethoven
composer.epithet: A pianist who turned small rhythmic cells into long arguments, then rebuilt the forms that contained them.
facts: Christian Gottlob Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Johann Georg Albrechtsberger and Antonio Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792 · Vienna and its surrounding villages thereafter
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · one opera
Progressive hearing loss documented in letters from 1801; conversation books used from 1818
composer.background:
Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770, probably on 16 December, and baptised on 17 December. His father Johann sang in the electoral court chapel, and his grandfather Ludwig had been its Kapellmeister. The family name came from the Low Countries; the ‘van’ did not indicate nobility. Johann attempted to present his son as a child prodigy, but Beethoven’s more substantial training came from Christian Gottlob Neefe, who introduced him to Bach’s keyboard music and helped him obtain work as an organist. Playing viola in the court orchestra also gave him practical knowledge of instrumental and operatic repertory.

The Bonn years supplied more than a musical apprenticeship. The court of Elector Maximilian Franz, educated patrons and friends such as the Breuning family brought Beethoven into contact with Enlightenment literature and social ideas. After his mother’s death in 1787 and his father’s worsening incapacity, he assumed increasing responsibility for the household. In 1792 he left for Vienna to study with Haydn. The intended period of further training became permanent residence: the French occupation of Bonn in 1794 ended the old electoral establishment to which he might have returned.

composer.name: Franz Schubert
composer.epithet: A Viennese songwriter who made the piano an equal narrator, and carried the harmonic dislocations of the Lied into symphonies and chamber music.
facts: Vienna Stadtkonvikt, 1808–13; composition with Antonio Salieri, 1812–16
Assistant in his father’s school; music tutor to the Esterházy family at Zseliz in 1818 and 1824; thereafter chiefly an independent composer
Johann Michael Vogl · Josef von Spaun · Franz von Schober · Johann Mayrhofer · Moritz von Schwind
More than 600 songs; symphonies, chamber music, piano sonatas and duets, masses and music for the stage
composer.background:
Schubert grew up in a schoolmaster’s household in Himmelpfortgrund, then a suburb of Vienna. His father taught him violin, his brother Ignaz taught him piano, and the parish musician Michael Holzer supplied further instruction. Family quartet sessions put Franz on viola, between the melody and the bass: he knew chamber music from an inner part. In 1808 he entered the imperial chapel choir and the Stadtkonvikt boarding school. Its orchestra introduced him to Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven as a player, while Antonio Salieri began giving him composition lessons in 1812.

After leaving the school in 1813, he trained as a teacher and became an assistant in his father’s classroom. Composition continued around the timetable. Gretchen am Spinnrade, dated 19 October 1814, gives Goethe’s girl a right-hand spinning wheel, a left-hand treadle and a vocal line that repeatedly tries to escape them. Schubert was seventeen. In 1815 he wrote roughly 140 songs, including Erlkönig, as well as symphonies, church music and stage works. Voice and piano already carried distinct dramatic responsibilities in his songs.

intro: The right hand has two jobs: carrying the melody and keeping the broken chords in motion underneath it. Schubert makes a single pianist sustain a singer, an accompaniment and a bass line at three different levels of weight.

composer.name: Hector Berlioz
composer.epithet: He made orchestral colour, the position of a sound in space, and the return of a remembered melody into structural events.
facts: Flute and guitar as a boy; Paris Conservatoire with Jean-François Le Sueur and Anton Reicha
Critic for the Journal des débats; Conservatoire librarian; touring conductor
Shakespeare, Goethe and Virgil supplied the subjects of his largest works
Four symphonies; operas; dramatic and sacred choral works; songs; an orchestration treatise
composer.background:
Berlioz grew up in La Côte-Saint-André, between Lyon and Grenoble, in the household of a physician who taught him Latin and expected him to study medicine. He learned flute and guitar, but never acquired the pianist’s routine of composing at a keyboard. Virgil’s account of Dido’s death affected him as a schoolboy; forty years later he would set it in Les Troyens. Sent to Paris in 1821, he attended anatomy lectures while spending his evenings at the Opéra. The theatre’s performances of Gluck offered a different education: declamation, orchestral gesture and the pacing of a dramatic scene.

He abandoned medicine, studied with Jean-François Le Sueur and entered the Conservatoire in 1826. His first large works included a Messe solennelle and the unfinished opera Les Francs-juges, whose overture survived independently. The Prix de Rome required a prescribed cantata; Berlioz finally won it in 1830, on his fourth attempt. The prize sent him to the Villa Medici, but the decisive musical experiences had already happened in Paris. Conservatoire performances under François-Antoine Habeneck introduced him to Beethoven’s symphonies, while an English theatrical company introduced him to Shakespeare.

era.name: Romanticism
era.heroCaption: Caspar David Friedrich, Two Men Contemplating the Moon

movement: IV. Marche au supplice — Allegretto non troppo
intro: Berlioz makes an execution march the fourth movement of a symphony. Low strings, brass and percussion turn a regular tread into public spectacle; one remembered melody interrupts the machinery.

cues.title: An execution in a dream
cues.text: This is the fourth of five movements. In Berlioz’s printed programme, an opium-dazed musician dreams that he has murdered his beloved and is being led to execution; the quiet opening prepares the procession rather than announcing a triumphant march.

cues.title: The melody walks down
cues.text: Cellos and double basses carry a descending march tune. Its weight comes from the low register and repeated steps; the answering orchestral accents interrupt rather than smooth out the line.

cues.title: An actress in Paris
cues.text: Berlioz saw Harriet Smithson as Ophelia and Juliet in Paris in 1827. She inspired the symphony’s beloved, but did not attend its premiere; hearing the revised work in December 1832 brought them together. They married in October 1833.

cues.title: The brass take command
cues.text: The march becomes louder and more openly ceremonial. The brass-led tune turns towards B♭ major, the relative major of G minor: the same two-flat key signature can support both the prisoner’s heavy steps and the procession’s public display.

cues.title: Paris hears the symphony
cues.text: François-Antoine Habeneck conducted the premiere at the Paris Conservatoire on 5 December 1830. Berlioz later recalled that the march took the audience by storm; his account also admits that two rehearsals had not been enough.

cues.title: Back to the low tread
cues.text: The volume drops and the darker march material returns. Listen to how quickly Berlioz rebuilds the sound: the withdrawal lasts only a few phrases before the full orchestral weight presses forward again.

cues.title: A march with a past
cues.text: In his memoirs Berlioz says he wrote this movement in one night. The manuscript supplies a qualification: he reworked a guards’ march from his abandoned opera Les Francs-juges. The remembered beloved was added for the symphony.

cues.title: A thought before the blow
cues.text: The march breaks off for a quiet recollection. A solo clarinet gives the opening of the idée fixe, the melody representing the beloved throughout the symphony; listen for how little of it the orchestra allows to survive.

cues.title: The sentence is carried out
cues.text: The orchestral blow cuts across the recollection. Brass and percussion turn the ending into a blunt G major proclamation: the bright final chord belongs to the crowd’s celebration, not to a reprieve for the condemned man.

cues.title: Four movements are not enough
cues.text: The final chords decay, but the symphony has one movement left. The witches’ sabbath will bring the beloved’s melody back on E♭ clarinet, stripped of its earlier singing character.

composer.name: Felix Mendelssohn
composer.epithet: A composer-conductor who turned quicksilver string writing, Bachian counterpoint and remembered landscapes into tightly organised concert music.
facts: Piano with Ludwig Berger; composition with Carl Friedrich Zelter in Berlin
Music director, Düsseldorf, 1833–35; Gewandhaus conductor, Leipzig, from 1835; founder of Leipzig Conservatoire, 1843
Brother of Fanny Hensel; married Cécile Jeanrenaud in 1837; five children
Symphonies, concert overtures, concertos, oratorios, chamber music and Songs without Words
composer.background:
Felix Mendelssohn was born in Hamburg in 1809 and grew up in Berlin, where his father Abraham’s banking wealth supported an unusually extensive education. His grandfather was the Jewish philosopher Moses Mendelssohn; Felix and his siblings were baptised as Christians in 1816, and the family used the additional surname Bartholdy. He studied piano with Ludwig Berger and composition with Carl Friedrich Zelter, alongside his elder sister Fanny. The family’s concerts extended their classroom education with repeated opportunities to hear their own music, revise it and discuss it with experienced performers.

Zelter’s teaching joined Bach’s counterpoint to classical forms. The boy wrote string symphonies, concertos and chamber works before the pieces usually treated as his starting point. At sixteen he composed the E♭ major Octet, Op. 20, for four violins, two violas and two cellos. Its eight independent parts create different densities inside one ensemble: the first violin’s long ascent, the other instruments’ pulsing accompaniments and the finale’s fugal entries continually reshape the texture. The scherzo’s soft, rapid articulation became a recurrent technical problem in his later orchestral writing.

era.name: Romanticism
era.heroCaption: Caspar David Friedrich, Two Men Contemplating the Moon

intro: A falling figure in the bassoons and lower strings generates an entire concert overture. Mendelssohn keeps its outline recognisable while changing the harmony, register and weight around it.

cues.title: Begin below the violins
cues.text: Bassoons, violas and cellos introduce the falling figure in B minor. It begins after a rest, so the pulse is already moving when the melody appears; listen for that small gap each time the figure returns.

cues.title: Before entering the cave
cues.text: On 7 August 1829 Mendelssohn sent his family a letter containing the overture’s opening twenty-one bars. He visited Fingal’s Cave the following day. The musical sketch therefore preceded the celebrated visit, rather than being composed inside the cave.

cues.title: A figure beneath the surface
cues.text: Throughout the opening, follow the short descending figure rather than only the highest melody. Its repetitions supply continuity while changing harmonies and orchestral layers prevent it from becoming a fixed accompaniment.

cues.title: A longer singing phrase
cues.text: The lyrical second subject expands the short opening gesture into a longer line. The harmony moves towards D major, B minor’s relative major, while the accompaniment retains the motion that made the opening restless.

cues.title: Two rates of movement
cues.text: Listen beneath the broad melody for the smaller moving notes. Mendelssohn separates melodic pace from accompanimental activity: a phrase can seem to float even while the instruments underneath it keep working.

cues.title: The first large crest
cues.text: The orchestral sound gathers weight. The following half-minute brings the loudest sustained passage of this recording; the compact opening material can now carry a whole ensemble rather than a low-register murmur.

cues.title: An overture without an opera
cues.text: The Hebrides was written for the concert hall, not to introduce a stage work. Its first performance took place in London on 14 May 1832; Mendelssohn continued revising the score after that performance.

cues.title: The development opens out
cues.text: The large orchestral crest subsides, and the harmony starts moving through less settled territory. This is development: familiar fragments are recombined and moved into new surroundings rather than replaced by a new main tune.

cues.title: The bass changes the view
cues.text: Listen to the low notes under the recurring material. Changes there alter the harmonic meaning of a familiar contour; the overture can move far from B minor without abandoning its opening vocabulary.

cues.title: Turner visits Staffa
cues.text: Turner visited Staffa in 1831, two years after Mendelssohn, and exhibited Staffa, Fingal’s Cave in 1832. His painting includes a steamship. The supposedly remote landscape was already a destination reached through modern transport.

cues.title: A sudden change of weight
cues.text: A brief swell gives way to a much darker-coloured orchestral sound. Listen for the difference between volume and colour: a passage can become less bright without disappearing or losing its forward motion.

cues.title: Repeated attacks gather force
cues.text: The texture becomes more insistently articulated. Repeated short attacks give the music a firmer tread, and the gradual increase in volume turns that articulation into another orchestral build-up.

cues.title: Keep the contour in mind
cues.text: Through this louder passage, keep the opening’s downward contour in memory. Sonata form makes recognition a practical listening task: the return matters because a short idea has remained traceable through the development.

cues.title: The opening ground returns
cues.text: The sound withdraws and the opening material returns around B minor. This recapitulation restores the overture’s starting ground, but it does not simply replay the earlier sequence unchanged.

cues.title: The orchestra draws back
cues.text: The volume falls further. In this exposed passage, small changes of attack and balance matter more than the size of the orchestra; listen for how a quiet line remains audible without being forced.

cues.title: Building a musical institution
cues.text: Mendelssohn became conductor of Leipzig’s Gewandhaus concerts in 1835. In 1843 he founded the Leipzig Conservatoire. Composing, rehearsing an orchestra and organising musical education belonged to the same working life.

cues.title: The closing drive begins
cues.text: The quiet span gives way to sharper attacks and a growing orchestral sound. B minor reasserts itself as the overture approaches its close; the familiar material now has less space between its surges.

cues.title: Follow the separate attacks
cues.text: Listen for the separation between notes inside the fuller sound. Mendelssohn’s fast orchestral writing needs coordinated articulation as well as volume; blurring the attacks would hide the smaller figures that carry the movement.

cues.title: One more gathering of force
cues.text: The sound swells once more before the final withdrawal. The overture does not maintain its orchestral weight to the last instant: its ending makes room for the low, falling material to be heard without that mass.

cues.title: The figure outlasts the surge
cues.text: The closing sound contracts into B minor. After the full-orchestra passages, the reduced ending makes the opening figure’s small scale audible again.

composer.name: Frédéric Chopin
composer.born: 1 March 1810, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.

intro: Chopin gives the piano the title of a narrative poem without supplying a plot. Two themes return in altered proportions, and a fast coda overturns the measured pace of the opening.

intro: A rocking left hand supports a melody that repeatedly grows a second voice. Listen for the difference between the notes that carry the phrase and the ornaments that delay their arrival.

composer.name: Robert Schumann
composer.epithet: His music lets remembered fragments, concealed names and competing inner voices interrupt the forms that contain them.
facts: Piano with Friedrich Wieck; composition with Heinrich Dorn; extensive private study of Bach and Beethoven
Co-founder of the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, 1834; editor until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
Leipzig Conservatoire teacher; municipal music director, Düsseldorf, 1850–53
composer.background:
Schumann grew up in Zwickau, where his father August was a bookseller and publisher. Reading and music developed together: Jean Paul’s novels, with their interruptions, doubles and changes of narrative voice, mattered alongside piano lessons. Sent to Leipzig to study law in 1828, he spent more time on music and literature; a period in Heidelberg did not reconcile him to a legal career. He returned to Leipzig to study piano seriously with Friedrich Wieck. Wieck’s daughter Clara, already performing publicly as a child, gave him an immediate example of the professional discipline he hoped to acquire.

A persistent problem with his right hand ended the prospect of a virtuoso career. The familiar account of a finger-strengthening device leaves the injury’s medical cause uncertain. Composition and criticism became his principal occupations. The early published piano works already had distinct literary and formal premises: the Abegg Variations derive a theme from letters, while Papillons relates its dances to the masked-ball ending of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre. The miniatures’ sudden juxtapositions recreate the experience of a narrative changing speakers and levels.

era.name: Romanticism
era.heroCaption: Caspar David Friedrich, Two Men Contemplating the Moon

work: Piano Concerto in A minor, Op. 54
performers: Sviatoslav Richter, Witold Rowicki, Warsaw National Philharmonic Orchestra
intro: The piano interrupts the orchestra almost before it has begun; then soloist and woodwind share a melody. Schumann builds his concerto around exchanges of material rather than a succession of solo displays.

composer.name: Franz Liszt
composer.born: 22 October 1811, Doborján, Kingdom of Hungary (now Raiding, Austria)
composer.epithet: The touring pianist who made a single theme change character, and eventually stripped virtuosity down to a few unresolved notes.
facts: Piano with Carl Czerny and composition with Antonio Salieri in Vienna; later composition with Anton Reicha in Paris
Weimar masterclasses; first president of the Hungarian Royal Academy of Music, founded in 1875
Piano music and transcriptions; thirteen symphonic poems; two programme symphonies; concertos, songs and sacred music
composer.background:
Liszt was born in Doborján, a German-speaking village in the Hungarian kingdom, where his father Adam worked on an Esterházy estate. Hungary remained his declared homeland, although German and French were his principal languages. Adam taught him piano before taking him to Vienna in 1822 for lessons with Carl Czerny, who had studied with Beethoven, and Antonio Salieri. The family moved to Paris the following year. The Conservatoire refused him admission as a foreigner; private teaching and public concerts supplied his education instead. His early career therefore joined two institutions that would remain distinct in his adult life: the disciplined lesson and the commercial concert platform.

Adam died in 1827, leaving the sixteen-year-old Liszt to support himself and his mother by teaching. Paris offered an education beyond the keyboard: Victor Hugo, the religious social thinker Félicité de Lamennais, Chopin and Berlioz belonged to his intellectual or musical circle. Hearing Paganini in 1832 suggested that a pianist might make technical difficulty carry the same theatrical force as the violinist’s leaps and harmonics. Liszt responded with prolonged practice and transcription: his piano version of Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique, published in 1834, aimed to preserve orchestral detail.

era.name: Romanticism
era.heroCaption: Caspar David Friedrich, Two Men Contemplating the Moon

intro: Four sharply separated sections turn a piano into a band: march, quick dance, slow declamation and a finale driven by repeated octaves. Argerich makes the changes of pace as conspicuous as the changes of register.

composer.name: Giuseppe Verdi
composer.born: 10 October 1813, Le Roncole, near Busseto (then in the French Empire)
composer.epithet: An opera composer who made a change of vocal phrase, bass note or ensemble balance alter the relations between people on stage.
facts: Ferdinando Provesi in Busseto; private study with Vincenzo Lavigna in Milan after rejection by the Conservatoire
La Scala, Milan · La Fenice, Venice · Paris Opéra · theatres in Naples, Rome, St Petersburg and Cairo
Francesco Maria Piave, Salvadore Cammarano and Arrigo Boito among his principal librettists
Operas from Oberto (1839) to Falstaff (1893); the Requiem, sacred pieces, songs and a string quartet
composer.background:
Verdi was born in Le Roncole, near Busseto, where his parents kept an inn and shop. He learnt the organ locally and studied with Ferdinando Provesi in Busseto. The merchant and amateur musician Antonio Barezzi helped finance further training in Milan, but the Conservatoire rejected him in 1832. Private study with Vincenzo Lavigna, who had worked at La Scala, gave him access to counterpoint and practical theatrical knowledge instead. In 1836 he married Barezzi’s daughter Margherita and took up municipal musical duties in Busseto. His route to opera passed through a provincial network of patronage, church work and teaching.

The first opera, Oberto, reached La Scala in 1839 and secured further commissions. By then Verdi had lost his daughter Virginia; his son Icilio died that year, and Margherita died in 1840. The comedy Un giorno di regno failed at La Scala in September 1840. Nabucco brought success in March 1842. Temistocle Solera’s libretto offered large public scenes, sharply opposed groups and an exiled people whose collective song could carry a dramatic burden usually assigned to a principal singer.

era.name: Romanticism
era.heroCaption: Caspar David Friedrich, Two Men Contemplating the Moon

intro: Before the party starts, Verdi gives Violetta an orchestral portrait: exposed high strings, then the melody she will sing when she leaves Alfredo. Toscanini recorded this complete prelude in Carnegie Hall in 1929.

composer.name: Richard Wagner
composer.epithet: An opera composer who made the orchestra remember what the characters conceal, and built a theatre for the result.
facts: Composition with Theodor Weinlig in Leipzig; practical theatre work in Würzburg, Magdeburg, Königsberg and Riga
Royal Saxon Kapellmeister, Dresden, 1843–49; founder of the Bayreuth Festival, first held in 1876
Wrote his own librettos, alongside extensive and often polemical prose
Thirteen completed operas; the four-part Ring; songs, orchestral works and piano music
composer.background:
Wagner grew up among actors, singers and theatrical households in Leipzig and Dresden. His father died in 1813; his mother subsequently married the actor and painter Ludwig Geyer. Literature preceded serious musical training: as a schoolboy Wagner attempted a tragedy before he had mastered composition. Beethoven’s symphonies and Weber’s operas supplied different models, one for the weight of an orchestral argument, the other for a German theatre of supernatural events and sharply characterised instruments. Lessons with Theodor Weinlig in 1831 gave him a grounding in counterpoint. The later claim to have rebuilt opera came from someone who first learned its routines as a working theatre musician.

He held posts in Würzburg, Magdeburg, Königsberg and Riga, married the actress Minna Planer in 1836, and repeatedly found himself in debt. His early operas tried incompatible languages: Die Feen follows German Romantic opera, while Das Liebesverbot, after Shakespeare’s Measure for Measure, adopts a more Italianate manner. In 1839 the Wagners fled Riga and travelled by sea to London, then to Paris. There he copied, arranged and wrote journalism while trying to enter the operatic establishment. Meyerbeer, whom Wagner would later attack, helped him obtain a hearing for Rienzi. Wagner knew the grand-opera machinery of public ceremony, political catastrophe and large chorus from practical experience.

era.heroCaption: Caspar David Friedrich, Two Men Contemplating the Moon

intro: A pilgrims’ hymn frames the restless music of Venus’s mountain. This concert-band arrangement puts Wagner’s opposition between sustained chorale and rushing figuration into wind and brass alone.

composer.name: Anton Bruckner
composer.epithet: A church organist who built symphonic movements from long harmonic spans, separate instrumental blocks and the silences between them.
facts: St Florian; harmony and counterpoint with Simon Sechter, 1855–61; form and orchestration with Otto Kitzler, 1861–63
Organist at St Florian and Linz Cathedral; Vienna Conservatory teacher from 1868; University of Vienna lecturer from 1875
Nine numbered symphonies, two earlier symphonies outside that sequence, masses, motets and other choral works
Several symphonies survive in distinct authorial versions, which later editors have treated differently
composer.background:
Bruckner was born in Ansfelden, near Linz, where his father was a schoolmaster and church musician. Teaching, organ playing and the parish liturgy belonged to the same local profession. After his father’s death in 1837, he became a choirboy at the Augustinian abbey of St Florian. The abbey gave him daily contact with sacred music and a large organ, but his first adult qualification was as a schoolteacher. He worked in small Upper Austrian communities before returning to St Florian in 1845. The later symphonist emerged from this practical church-and-school environment.

He became the abbey’s organist and moved to Linz Cathedral in 1855. By then he was thirty-one, yet he submitted himself to six further years of harmony and counterpoint study with Simon Sechter in Vienna, much of it conducted through written exercises and correspondence. Sechter’s discipline discouraged free composition while the technical work continued. Bruckner sought formal certification even after he had become an accomplished organ improviser. This extended apprenticeship matters when hearing a symphonic climax: its apparent mass rests on carefully managed lines, prepared dissonances and a bass that controls the rate of harmonic change.

era.name: Romanticism
era.heroCaption: Caspar David Friedrich, Two Men Contemplating the Moon

work: Symphony No. 7 in E major, WAB 107
movement: III. Scherzo — Sehr schnell; Trio — Etwas langsamer
performers: University of Music and Theatre Munich
intro: The Seventh’s scherzo compresses Bruckner’s block-like construction into nine minutes. A repeated string figure and a trumpet call drive the outer sections; the slower trio changes both their pace and their weight.

composer.name: Johannes Brahms
composer.epithet: A composer who made a small interval generate a large form, and let conflicting rhythms keep a familiar melody unsettled.
facts: Piano with Otto Friedrich Willibald Cossel; piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen in Hamburg
Seasonal work in Detmold, 1857–59; Vienna Singakademie, 1863–64; Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde concerts, 1872–75
Based in Vienna; summer composition in Baden-Baden, Pörtschach, Mürzzuschlag and Bad Ischl
Four symphonies, four concertos, chamber music, piano music, songs and choral works; no opera
composer.background:
Brahms was born in Hamburg, the son of a professional musician, Johann Jakob Brahms, who played several instruments, and Christiane Nissen, a seamstress. His father supplied an introduction to practical music-making; Otto Friedrich Willibald Cossel and Eduard Marxsen gave him systematic piano and composition lessons. The young Brahms played for income and learned the trade from inside, accompanying, arranging and performing. Marxsen’s teaching connected keyboard technique with the study of Bach, Mozart and Beethoven. Those composers supplied working materials: Brahms’s later scores are full of old procedures subjected to new rhythmic pressure.

In 1853 he toured with the Hungarian violinist Ede Reményi and met Joseph Joachim, who became a lifelong collaborator. Joachim sent him to Robert and Clara Schumann in Düsseldorf. Robert’s article “Neue Bahnen”, published that October, announced the twenty-year-old as a major new figure before his music was widely available. The endorsement opened publishers’ doors and imposed an awkward expectation of scale. His early piano sonatas, already orchestral in weight and contrast, could be treated as promises of symphonies he had not yet written. Brahms responded by publishing selectively and destroying much of the work he did not wish to preserve.

work: Symphony No. 3 in F major, Op. 90
intro: Instead of a scherzo, Brahms writes a C minor song in three beats. The melody passes between strings and winds; changes of instrumental colour do the work that louder music might give to a climax.

intro: Brahms ends his last symphony with thirty variations on an eight-bar pattern derived from Bach. The repeating foundation survives changes of rhythm, register and orchestration, but the final cadence refuses the customary escape into the major.

composer.name: Modest Mussorgsky
composer.epithet: He made Russian speech, public crowds and the noises of ordinary life determine the shape of opera.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition informally with Mily Balakirev; no conservatory education
Guards officer until 1858; civil servant, including work in the Forestry Department
Balakirev, Borodin, Cui and Rimsky-Korsakov; the critic Vladimir Stasov
Operas, dramatic songs and piano music; many works unfinished or published in other composers’ revisions
composer.background:
Mussorgsky grew up on his family’s estate at Karevo, where his mother taught him the piano and his nurse supplied stories that he later associated with his earliest improvisations. The household belonged to the landowning class. The peasant voices he eventually put into songs and operas came from another social world. Sent to Saint Petersburg for schooling, he studied piano with Anton Gerke and entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852. In 1856 he joined the Preobrazhensky Regiment. His first published piano piece, a polka, belonged to the drawing room.

Meeting Dargomyzhsky and then Balakirev redirected that education. Balakirev taught through playing, criticism and the examination of scores. Mussorgsky left the army in 1858, but composing did not provide a living. The emancipation of the serfs in 1861 disrupted the estate income on which his family depended, and he eventually took civil-service posts. The group later called the Five brought together different professions and musical methods: Borodin was a chemist, Cui a military engineer, Rimsky-Korsakov a naval officer. Their shared opposition to imported academic authority concealed substantial musical disagreements.

era.name: Romanticism
era.heroCaption: Caspar David Friedrich, Two Men Contemplating the Moon

intro: A witches’ gathering interrupted by a church bell. This is Rimsky-Korsakov’s 1886 concert version, assembled after Mussorgsky’s death, not the orchestral score Mussorgsky finished in 1867.

cues.title: Motion before melody
cues.text: The opening builds its agitation from rapid string figures and sharply separated orchestral gestures. Listen for the difference between the moving surface and the heavier notes beneath it: the lower instruments do not simply double everything the strings play.

cues.title: An officer leaves service
cues.text: Mussorgsky entered the Preobrazhensky Guards in 1856 and left the army in 1858. He learnt composition informally from Balakirev rather than at a conservatory; his later employment included civil-service work.

cues.title: Smaller, quicker gestures
cues.text: The weight drops away, but the attacks become more frequent. Quietness does not mean rest: short figures keep the pulse active while the orchestra sheds some of its mass.

cues.title: A sudden change of scale
cues.text: Keep the quiet dance in your ear as the volume increases. The change comes through orchestral weight rather than a complete halt and a new beginning.

cues.title: The upper edge sharpens
cues.text: The sound becomes brighter in the coming phrase. Follow the high activity separately from the lower accents: the two layers give the music different kinds of momentum.

cues.title: Another short-lived crest
cues.text: A quick crescendo pushes the orchestra forward, then releases it. Mussorgsky’s material can work in these compact blocks: a repeated figure, an increase in weight, a sudden change of texture.

cues.title: Balakirev rejects the score
cues.text: Mussorgsky finished his original orchestral version in 1867. Balakirev rejected it, and it was not performed in Mussorgsky’s lifetime. The music survived through several further attempts to place the witches’ gathering in a stage work.

cues.title: A different harmonic field
cues.text: The harmony moves away from the opening’s D-centred writing. Listen for a broader line and slower changes of emphasis: a new span is being built rather than another immediate burst.

cues.title: Sustaining the pressure
cues.text: Listen beneath the louder gestures for repeated notes and held support. They allow the upper parts to change shape without making the music feel as though it has started again.

cues.title: The volume breaks upward
cues.text: The phrase reaches a forceful crest, falls back and prepares a still stronger one. Repeated surges, rather than one uninterrupted crescendo, make the gathering increasingly crowded.

cues.title: An editor’s concert piece
cues.text: Rimsky-Korsakov completed this version in 1886, five years after Mussorgsky’s death. He drew on the composer’s later stage versions as well as the earlier material; this is a reconstruction and recomposition, not merely a new orchestration of the 1867 score.

cues.title: Pressure in successive waves
cues.text: The orchestra keeps rebuilding its volume after brief withdrawals. Notice how each new increase also sharpens the upper sound: loudness and brightness reinforce one another without remaining constant.

cues.title: A low starting point
cues.text: The texture suddenly becomes quieter and darker. This is not the ending: the orchestra uses the reduction as the beginning of another climb.

cues.title: Before the interruption
cues.text: Listen for the contrast between this renewed orchestral force and the stillness that follows. The fast section reaches one of its brightest peaks before the whole pattern is broken.

cues.title: The gathering disperses
cues.text: The fast music breaks off. The church bell belongs to the score’s change from the witches’ gathering to daybreak; the orchestral activity gives way to a long, quiet aftermath.

cues.title: An unfinished comic opera
cues.text: Mussorgsky reused the sabbath music in his unfinished opera The Fair at Sorochyntsi, after Gogol. The dream sequence there helped supply the materials from which Rimsky-Korsakov made the familiar concert ending.

cues.title: Listen for the bass
cues.text: The low D gives these quiet phrases a fixed reference point. Attend to how little movement is needed above a sustained foundation; the same orchestra that crowded the fast section can now leave a single line exposed.

cues.title: A minor-key shadow
cues.text: The quiet ending is not harmonically motionless. A darker inflection briefly colours the D-centred music before the major sonority settles again.

cues.title: Repin at the hospital
cues.text: In 1881 Ilya Repin painted Mussorgsky in the Nikolaevsky Military Hospital in Saint Petersburg. The composer died there that March, shortly after his forty-second birthday; the portrait records the hospital gown rather than the uniform of his youth.

cues.title: Resonance without the rush
cues.text: The lower, softer sound carries almost no rapid attacks. Listen to the spaces between changes: the close is sustained by resonance and small shifts of harmony, not by the running figures of the opening.

cues.title: A major-key ending
cues.text: The closing sonority remains centred on D major. The piece that began with restless, conflicting lines ends with the bass and upper harmony agreeing on the same tonic.

composer.name: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
composer.epithet: He used the timing of dance and theatre to make a symphony’s return, interruption or collapse physically audible.
facts: Imperial School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck supplied an allowance from 1877 to 1890; their correspondence became a major record of his working life
Six numbered symphonies and Manfred; three ballets; operas, concertos, chamber music, piano music and songs
composer.background:
Tchaikovsky was born at Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. Music belonged to the household before it became a profession: his governess Fanny Dürbach remembered the child’s intense responses to it, and he began piano lessons early. His formal training nevertheless pointed towards government service. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg, separated from his family. His mother died of cholera in 1854. After graduating in 1859 he worked in the Ministry of Justice, while concerts, opera and lessons gradually occupied more of his time.

When Anton Rubinstein’s Saint Petersburg Conservatory opened in 1862, Tchaikovsky joined its first generation of students. He studied composition with Rubinstein and theoretical subjects with Nikolai Zaremba, leaving government employment in 1863. The training mattered practically: he could organise large forms, prepare orchestral scores and teach harmony. In 1866 Nikolai Rubinstein recruited him for the new Moscow Conservatory. Tchaikovsky taught there until 1878, wrote criticism and translated pedagogical material. His early reputation grew through this sustained professional work.

composer.name: Antonín Dvořák
composer.epithet: A theatre violist who made dance accents, remembered songs and classical development work inside the same movement.
facts: Local teachers in Bohemia; Prague Organ School, 1857–59
Violist in Prague’s Provisional Theatre orchestra, 1862–71; organist and private teacher
Prague Conservatory; director of the National Conservatory of Music in New York, 1892–95
Nine symphonies, operas, concertos, chamber music, choral works and songs; B numbers refer to Jarmil Burghauser’s catalogue
composer.background:
Dvořák was born in Nelahozeves, a village north of Prague, where his father kept an inn and worked as a butcher. He learnt violin locally and acquired further musical training at Zlonice before attending the Prague Organ School in 1857–59. He earned his living in ensembles, including the orchestra of Prague’s Provisional Theatre from 1862 to 1871, playing viola under conductors who included Smetana. Opera taught him how a middle part supports singers, how repeated figures sustain a scene and how instrumental colour carries across a crowded theatre.

His early compositions were extensive and often ambitious: chamber music, symphonies and operatic projects accumulated before he had a dependable publisher. Wagner’s influence is audible in the scale and harmonic movement of some of these works. In 1873 he married Anna Čermáková. Teaching and an organist’s post helped support the household while applications for an Austrian state stipend brought his scores to influential readers. The award first received in 1875 brought both honour and money at a point when publication and commissions remained uncertain.

era.heroCaption: Caspar David Friedrich, Two Men Contemplating the Moon

work: Symphony No. 9 in E minor “From the New World”, Op. 95
intro: The cor anglais melody became “Goin’ Home” only after Dvořák’s death. Around that apparently simple song he builds a slow movement with a minor-key middle, a sudden orchestral confrontation and a retreat into chamber music.

composer.name: Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov
composer.epithet: A naval officer turned teacher who made orchestral register and symmetrical scales the machinery of Russian fairy-tale opera.
facts: Naval College in Saint Petersburg; composition with Mily Balakirev, followed by intensive private study
Saint Petersburg Conservatory from 1871; inspector of naval bands, 1873–84
Married the pianist and composer Nadezhda Purgold in 1872; she assisted with arrangements and editorial work
Fifteen operas, three symphonies, orchestral suites and overtures, songs and teaching books
composer.background:
Rimsky-Korsakov was born in Tikhvin into a family with a tradition of naval service. He entered the Naval College in Saint Petersburg in 1856, while continuing piano lessons and attending opera. His teacher Fyodor Kanille introduced him to Balakirev in 1861. The young officer began a symphony before he had the theoretical equipment expected of a conservatory composition student. A naval voyage on the clipper Almaz took him abroad in 1862–65, interrupting regular contact with the circle while work on the symphony continued. Balakirev conducted the First Symphony in Saint Petersburg in 1865.

His early colleagues included Mussorgsky, Borodin and Cui. With Balakirev they became the group known as the Five, united by friendship and cultural argument despite their differing methods. Rimsky-Korsakov’s orchestral picture Sadko, first written in 1867, already connects a supernatural subject with an unusual pitch organisation. The sea musician’s underwater world encouraged scales and chord relationships outside ordinary major and minor. His experience of ships and oceans gave the subject a biographical setting.

movement: III. The Young Prince and the Young Princess
performers: San Francisco Symphony Orchestra, Pierre Monteux; Naoum Blinder, violin
intro: A string melody and a lighter dance occupy the third movement of this orchestral suite. The solo violin belongs to the storytelling frame: Rimsky-Korsakov warns against assigning a separate plot incident to every musical detail.

composer.name: Gabriel Fauré
composer.epithet: A church organist who made the French song and the chamber ensemble laboratories for harmony.
facts: École Niedermeyer, 1854–65; piano with Camille Saint-Saëns
Madeleine: choirmaster 1877–96, organist 1896–1905 · Paris Conservatoire: composition professor 1896–1905, director 1905–20
Mélodies, piano music, chamber music, Requiem, the opera Pénélope
composer.background:
Fauré learned his trade in a school for church musicians. His father was a schoolmaster in the Ariège; at nine, Gabriel was sent to Louis Niedermeyer’s recently founded school in Paris, where plainchant, Renaissance polyphony, organ playing and counterpoint belonged to the ordinary curriculum. The education matters to the harmony. A melody can cadence in minor with an unsharpened seventh degree; a chord can emerge from the independent movement of voices. These possibilities were practical knowledge before they became a recognisable Fauré style.

After Niedermeyer died in 1861, Camille Saint-Saëns took over the piano class and introduced the pupils to Schumann, Liszt and Wagner. Teacher and pupil remained friends for more than sixty years. Fauré’s graduation work, the Cantique de Jean Racine of 1865, already joins the two educations: a flowing keyboard accompaniment beneath a choral texture whose entries are controlled by contrapuntal discipline. Its French text is Racine’s paraphrase of a Latin hymn. The bass supports long phrases that carry the upper voices across the bar-lines.

era.name: The French Line
era.heroCaption: James McNeill Whistler, Nocturne: Blue and Gold — Old Battersea Bridge

performers: Chorale Philippe Caillard; Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo, Louis Frémaux
intro: The prayer for rest begins in F major, with a string melody that moves independently of the voices. Fauré then joins it to the Communion’s prayer for eternal light and recalls the opening of the Requiem itself.

cues.title: Two melodies, not one
cues.text: Before the voices, a moving string line establishes F major. When the tenors take up the prayer, that line does not stop: the accompaniment has a melody of its own.

cues.title: A school for church musicians
cues.text: Fauré entered the École Niedermeyer at nine. Plainchant and counterpoint belonged to his training; Saint-Saëns later taught him piano and introduced him to Schumann, Liszt and Wagner. The church musician and the experimental harmonist had the same education.

cues.title: The petition gains weight
cues.text: The fuller choir makes the plea more insistent. The string motion continues, but the chords beneath the words no longer keep the opening’s F major settled; changes of harmony supply the pressure without a change of basic pulse.

cues.title: The tenor line returns
cues.text: The tenors recover the opening prayer and the volume falls back. Follow the string line underneath: Fauré can restore the same melody without making its accompaniment merely double the singers.

cues.title: From rest to light
cues.text: The text turns to “Lux aeterna”: let eternal light shine upon them. The sopranos’ held note begins a new section; the harmony opens beneath it, replacing the earlier melody-and-accompaniment texture with sustained choral chords.

cues.title: An ordinary Paris funeral
cues.text: Fauré conducted the first version of the Requiem at the Madeleine on 16 January 1888, for the funeral of the architect Joseph Lesoufaché. It had five movements. The Offertoire and Libera me joined it later; the enlarged orchestral version followed in 1900.

cues.title: The choir holds together
cues.text: Listen to the weight of voices moving in chords rather than answering one another in imitation. The sustained choral sound grows stronger across this passage; the changing bass gives those long notes a direction.

cues.title: The whole Requiem remembered
cues.text: The prayer “Requiem aeternam” returns with music from the work’s opening movement. This is a quotation across movements, not another statement of the Agnus Dei tune: Fauré brings the larger work into this movement’s closing pages.

cues.title: One last choral swell
cues.text: The recollection grows into the movement’s strongest swell. Notice how briefly the choir holds that weight before the sound withdraws; the passage does not turn into a separate fast section.

cues.title: The teacher of Ravel
cues.text: In 1896 Fauré became composition professor at the Paris Conservatoire; his pupils included Ravel, Koechlin and Nadia Boulanger. He became its director in 1905, although he had never studied there. Hearing trouble had already begun in 1903.

cues.title: An ending without voices
cues.text: The voices have finished, leaving the orchestra to close the movement. The instrumental melody recalls the opening, but there is no final choral declaration: the last sound belongs to the accompaniment that was never merely an accompaniment.

composer.name: Leoš Janáček
composer.epithet: A Moravian composer who studied the inflections of speech and built operas from short cells, repeated figures and abrupt changes of perspective.
facts: Old Brno monastery choir; Prague Organ School; further study in Leipzig and Vienna
Teacher and choral conductor in Brno; founder and director of the Brno Organ School, 1881–1919
Moravian folk song · Czech speech · Russian literature · Gabriela Preissová, Rudolf Těsnohlídek and Karel Čapek
Nine operas; choral and orchestral works; two string quartets; piano music; folk-song collections
composer.background:
Janáček was born in Hukvaldy in 1854, into a Moravian schoolmaster’s family. At eleven he became a chorister at the Augustinian monastery in Old Brno, where Pavel Křížkovský supplied rigorous musical training. His education continued at the Prague Organ School and, more briefly, in Leipzig and Vienna. He returned to Brno to build his career. Teaching, conducting and organising institutions occupied much of his adult life: he founded the Brno Organ School in 1881 and directed it until 1919. The composer now associated with the modernist opera house spent decades preparing other people’s practical musical education.

He married Zdeňka Schulzová in 1881. Their son Vladimír died in childhood; their daughter Olga died in 1903, aged twenty-one. The marriage endured these losses but was repeatedly strained. Friendship with Dvořák and the repertory of Czech choral societies helped shape the earlier compositions, yet Janáček’s mature manner developed slowly. He was already in his forties when the short motives, irregular phrases and repeated accompaniment figures of his later music began to replace more conventional forms. His position in musical history is therefore misleading if determined only by his birth date, a decade before Strauss.

intro: Janáček wrote this sonata after a worker was killed during demonstrations for a Czech university in Brno. Its second movement builds from a short, returning piano phrase; the interruptions matter as much as the notes.

composer.name: Edward Elgar
composer.epithet: A Worcester violinist who made orchestral variations into portraits of friends and the concerto into an argument with memory.
facts: Largely self-taught; violin, organ, orchestral playing and his father’s Worcester music shop
Bandmaster, Worcester County Asylum, Powick, 1879–84 · organist, St George’s Catholic Church, 1885–89 · Master of the King’s Musick, 1924–34
Two completed symphonies; violin and cello concertos; choral works; chamber music; five completed Pomp and Circumstance marches
composer.background:
Elgar learned the orchestra from inside it. His father William kept a music shop in Worcester, tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church. Edward read the scores in the shop, played violin in local ensembles, taught several instruments and eventually succeeded his father at the organ. He was born in Lower Broadheath in 1857, a Catholic in a predominantly Anglican musical establishment and a tradesman’s son in a profession increasingly organised around London colleges. He remained sensitive to both distinctions throughout his later success. His practical education taught him how a phrase feels under a bow.

At Powick he wrote quadrilles and polkas for an unusual ensemble, learning to give each instrument useful work. The Three Choirs Festival brought larger repertory within reach: Handel, Mendelssohn and contemporary oratorio, alongside orchestral music from the Continent. Visits to London widened that education. Wagner mattered particularly: the chromatic connection between chords, the orchestral recollection of earlier events and the long postponement of a cadence all entered Elgar’s language. His mature scores acquired part of their English character through their subsequent public use.

work: Variations on an Original Theme “Enigma”, Op. 36
intro: A portrait of August Jaeger, the publisher’s reader who encouraged Elgar when he was close to giving up. The melody grows through repeated rises and withdrawals rather than a change of tempo.

composer.name: Giacomo Puccini
composer.epithet: An opera composer who made a remembered tune, a stage noise or a change of orchestral register determine the timing of a scene.
facts: Lucca; Milan Conservatory, 1880–83, with Antonio Bazzini and Amilcare Ponchielli
Publisher Giulio Ricordi · librettists Luigi Illica and Giuseppe Giacosa · later Giuseppe Adami and Renato Simoni
Twelve operas when the three parts of Il trittico are counted separately; songs, sacred and chamber music
composer.background:
Puccini was born into a dynasty of church musicians in Lucca in 1858. His father Michele died when Giacomo was five, and the expectation that the boy would inherit the family profession survived him. Puccini studied locally, played the organ and composed sacred music, including a Mass completed in 1880. Hearing Verdi’s Aida in Pisa in 1876 helped turn his attention towards the theatre. A scholarship enabled him to enter the Milan Conservatory in 1880, where he studied with Antonio Bazzini and Amilcare Ponchielli. His graduation work, the orchestral Capriccio sinfonico, already contains material he would reuse at the beginning of La bohème.

His first opera, Le Villi, failed to win the Sonzogno competition for which it was written, but a performance in Milan in 1884 attracted the publisher Giulio Ricordi. Ricordi supported revisions, further performances and the much less successful Edgar, premiered at La Scala in 1889. The partnership mattered because Puccini composed slowly, demanded repeated alterations to his texts and needed protection against a premature commercial verdict. The theatre was a collective workshop: librettist, publisher, designer and conductor all contributed practical decisions, although Puccini insisted on controlling the length and placement of the decisive moments.

intro: Mimì introduces herself to Rodolfo: she embroiders flowers, lives alone and waits for spring. Puccini lets ordinary conversation open into a long vocal line, then return to conversation.

composer.name: Gustav Mahler
composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.

era.name: Fin de siècle
era.heroCaption: Gustav Klimt, Beethoven Frieze: The Well-Armed Strong One

intro: The quiet centre of a loud symphony. After three movements for a full orchestra, Mahler sends home the winds, brass and percussion and writes ten minutes for strings and harp alone.

cues.title: Fourth of five movements
cues.text: The Fifth Symphony runs from a funeral march in C♯ minor to a D major finale. This Adagietto is the hinge before that finale, and the only movement without a single wind instrument.

cues.title: Strings, harp, almost no pulse
cues.text: Soft sustained strings and the harp’s broken chords set up F major. The pulse is so slow that each harmony seems to hang; the first violins’ melody enters above it and moves only when the chord underneath has been fully heard.

cues.title: Maiernigg, 1901
cues.text: Mahler composed the Fifth in the summers of 1901 and 1902 in his composing hut above the Wörthersee in Carinthia, during the years he ran the Vienna Court Opera. He composed only in summer; winters were for the opera house.

cues.title: Leaning notes
cues.text: Listen to how the melody’s important notes arrive: often on a note that clashes with the harmony and then slips by step onto a chord tone. These appoggiaturas, the musical equivalent of a sigh, carry most of the movement’s expression.

cues.title: A letter without words?
cues.text: The conductor Willem Mengelberg wrote in his score that the Adagietto was Mahler’s declaration of love to Alma Schindler, sent to her in manuscript instead of a letter. They met in November 1901 and married in March 1902. The story rests on Mengelberg’s word alone.

cues.title: The first climax
cues.text: The line climbs and the strings thicken. Around 3:00 comes the first big swell, the loudest passage so far, before the music falls back to a whisper.

cues.title: Home again
cues.text: F major returns, quiet and settled. Notice how much of the music’s weight sits in the cellos and basses here: the bass line is a melody in its own right.

cues.title: A darker swell
cues.text: The texture surges again and the harmony turns toward the minor, as if the first section were trying to break out of itself.

cues.title: Fließender: the middle section
cues.text: The marking changes to “more flowing” and the harmony slips into G♭ major, a semitone above F. A shift of a semitone keeps the same room and changes the light.

cues.title: Higher, brighter
cues.text: The violins move up and the sound gets brighter; the middle section builds to its own peak around 5:30 before turning again.

cues.title: The Rückert summer
cues.text: In August 1901, the same summer the Fifth was begun, Mahler set Rückert’s “Ich bin der Welt abhanden gekommen”: “I have become lost to the world.” The song is also in F major and also slow, and its sound world is very close to this movement’s. Of the song he said, “It is myself.”

cues.title: Wandering keys
cues.text: Before coming home the harmony travels through sharper regions. Mahler treats keys as colours to pass through, not as places to stay.

cues.title: The return
cues.text: The opening music comes back in F major, a little fuller than before. The return is the movement’s main event: you hear the same melody again, but now you have been somewhere else.

cues.title: A second life
cues.text: For decades the Adagietto was played on its own as a funeral piece. Leonard Bernstein conducted it at Robert Kennedy’s funeral in St Patrick’s Cathedral in 1968, and Visconti’s film Death in Venice (1971) made it famous far beyond the concert hall.

cues.title: How slow is slow?
cues.text: This performance takes about ten and a half minutes. Mengelberg, who knew Mahler, recorded it in 1926 in about seven; Bruno Walter, Mahler’s assistant, took under eight in 1938. Many modern conductors stretch it past eleven. The marking is only “Sehr langsam”.

cues.title: The final ascent
cues.text: The melody begins its last climb. From about 9:15 comes the loudest passage of the movement, the violins at the top of their line with the full string body behind them.

cues.title: Dissolve
cues.text: The sound thins and the last F major harmony fades into the hall.

cues.title: What comes next
cues.text: The Rondo-Finale begins with a solo horn and later turns this movement’s melody into something quick and light-footed. In the symphony, the love song becomes material for a comedy.
